title: Seventh Annual Report of the National Cataract Audit: National Cataract Audit for the 2022 NHS Year: 01 April 2022 to 31 March 2023
article_subtype: Prospective national clinical audit annual report
condition_or_topic: Quality and safety of cataract surgery, assessed through the National Cataract Audit
clinical_background: Cataract surgery is the most common NHS surgical procedure. Approximately 608,000 publicly funded operations were performed in England and 16,000 in Wales during the 2022 NHS year, at an estimated annual NHS cost of around £600 million. Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR) is an intraoperative complication associated with greater risk of ocular harm and impaired visual recovery. Vision Loss captures deterioration in vision related to surgery. Since 2010, recorded PCR has fallen by around 58% and assessable Vision Loss by 31%, but reliable assessment depends on sufficiently complete data, particularly preoperative and postoperative visual acuity measurements.
objectives: Assess the quality of cataract surgery for patients undergoing an operation because cataracts adversely affect their vision, and identify performance below what patients can reasonably expect.

Report risk-adjusted rates of PCR and Vision Loss as the primary patient-safety outcomes, drawing attention to preoperative risk assessment, potentially avoidable complications and unwarranted variation in visual harm.
Provide contextual measures of case complexity, surgical volume, data completeness and access to surgery, including preoperative visual acuity by centre and by deprivation.
Enable centres and surgeons to compare their outcomes with peers and use the findings to improve care.
study_design: Seventh prospective annual National Cataract Audit, based on routinely collected surgical and clinical records from participating centres. The audit assessed operations in the 2022 NHS year and compared selected measures with earlier NHS years; it did not assign treatments.

population.description: Adults undergoing eligible cataract surgery by phacoemulsification at 177 participating centres in England, Wales and Guernsey. The analysis included 481,530 operations involving 367,515 patients.
inclusion_criteria: Cataract operations performed between 01 April 2022 and 31 March 2023 in adults aged 18 or above.
Operations including phacoemulsification, a cataract indication, a surgeon identifier and a valid surgeon grade.
Operations meeting the audit's procedural and diagnostic eligibility rules at centres contributing at least 50 eligible cataract operations.
exclusion_criteria: Cataract operations not performed by phacoemulsification or performed for an ineligible indication.
Operations combined with another significant intraocular procedure, subject to the audit's specified exceptions for pars plana vitrectomy.
Operations for traumatic injury or in eyes previously damaged by ocular trauma, with polar cataract, or with significant congenital or developmental abnormalities.
Operations in individuals aged <18 years, or operations without the required surgeon information.
Centres contributing <50 eligible operations; additional minimum-volume and VA-data requirements applied to postoperative and Vision Loss estimates.
population.care_setting: Participating hospital ophthalmology services and independent-sector cataract surgery centres.

interventions: Cataract surgery including phacoemulsification, with or without IOL and other eligible accompanying procedures.
comparators: Results for first treated eyes, second treated eyes and ISBCS eyes.
Results by surgeon grade, participating centre, recorded ocular co-pathology or risk factor, and social deprivation.
Selected measures across NHS years, including comparisons with 2010 and the 2018 – 2022 NHS years.

primary: PCR: posterior capsule rupture with or without vitreous prolapse, or zonule rupture with vitreous prolapse, reported as a case-complexity-adjusted intraoperative adverse-event rate.

Vision Loss: surgery-related worsening of visual acuity, generally a loss of ≥0.30 LogMAR for eyes with preoperative VA <1.00 LogMAR, with separate criteria for eyes with poorer preoperative VA; reported as a case-complexity-adjusted rate.
secondary: Preoperative and postoperative VA, change in VA, and completeness of VA recording.
Other recorded intraoperative and postoperative complications, and severe VA loss defined as a loss of ≥0.60 LogMAR.
Case ascertainment, case complexity, access to surgery assessed using preoperative VA, and variation by deprivation and centre.

statistical_methods: PCR and Vision Loss rates were adjusted for case complexity using mixed effects logistic regression risk-prediction models. Centre-level adjusted funnel plots included 95% and 99.8% error lines, based on reference consultant rates of 1.1% for PCR and 0.9% for Vision Loss. An outlier was defined by a risk-adjusted adverse-event rate above the national threshold plus approximately three Standard Deviations (3SD). Case ascertainment was estimated against NHS Digital or DHCW operation counts, with a pro rata denominator for centres contributing for only part of the year. A centre or surgeon required at least 50 eligible operations for a result; reporting Vision Loss also required both preoperative and postoperative VA data for at least 60% of operations. A case complexity index represented the predicted probability of each adverse outcome from the reported case mix.
follow_up: PCR assessment covered operations from 01 April 2022 to 31 March 2023. Postoperative outcomes were restricted to operations performed from 01 April 2022 to 31 January 2023 to provide the potential for two months’ postoperative follow-up. Eligible preoperative VA measurements were taken within six months before surgery; postoperative VA measurements were taken between eight days and six months after surgery, inclusive.
interpretation: The authors consider cataract surgery across the 177 participating centres to be of generally good quality. In the 2022 NHS year, recorded PCR affected 0.79% of operations and assessable Vision Loss affected 0.48%; no surgeon or centre exceeded the national threshold by more than 3 standard deviations for either outcome. The authors regard the declines since 2010 as beneficial to patients, while cautioning that incomplete VA recording prevents confidence that poor visual outcomes have not been missed. They also view the reduced share of operations performed by trainees as a concern for future service quality and sustainability.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Within the audit's historical series, recorded PCR has fallen by around 58% and assessable Vision Loss by 31% since 2010. The report equates the decline in PCR complications to approximately 7,000 fewer complications across the NHS each year. The proportion of eligible operations performed by trainees fell from 21.9% in the 2018 NHS year to 11.5% in the 2022 NHS year; the authors note that greater representation of high-volume consultant-delivered services contributes to this change. They describe the distribution of operations across months in the 2021 and 2022 NHS years as more similar to the corresponding months in 2018 and 2019 than to the disrupted 2020 NHS year.
clinical_implications: PCR is associated with a substantially greater risk of ocular harm and can impair visual recovery; the audit therefore treats PCR and Vision Loss as complementary patient-safety measures.
The authors estimate that avoiding PCR complications saves the NHS around £3.5 million annually in additional treatment costs, while avoiding Vision Loss can benefit patients in everyday life.
Eyes with ocular co-pathology, an intraoperative complication or PCR had worse postoperative VA than eyes without those problems.
The association between greater social deprivation and worse preoperative VA suggests variation in access to surgery before visual impairment becomes advanced.
Incomplete preoperative and postoperative VA measurements increase uncertainty about visual outcomes and can prevent evaluation of centres or surgeons for Vision Loss.
The decline in trainee-performed operations raises concern about the training needed to maintain safe, high-quality cataract services.
practice_implications: Patients, carers and other interested people are encouraged to consult publicly available audit results for surgeons and centres. Patients whose local provider does not participate could ask the hospital why and request outcomes for comparison with national benchmarks.
Clinicians should discuss the audit's key outcomes during consent and use patient-specific PCR risk calculations as recommended in the NICE cataract surgery guideline (NG77).
All providers of NHS cataract surgery should submit audit data, review their centre results, agree actions for quality improvement and submit complete information on relevant risk factors.

Providers should use electronic data collection and EMR audit tools for continuous monitoring, and review care pathways to maximise preoperative and postoperative VA recording for every operation. They should aspire to routine collection of postoperative refractive outcomes.
Providers should consider collecting Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) before and after surgery, as advised in the 2019 NICE Quality standard for serious eye disorders (QS180).

EMR-enabled providers should review mandatory-field settings, make surgeon GMC number recording mandatory and verify trainee grades annually. Surgeons at non-participating centres should raise the case for participation with senior management.

Commissioners should specify complete submission to the RCOphth NOD audit, including preoperative and postoperative VA, in cataract-service contracts. Where postoperative care is outsourced, services should require VA and refraction data to be returned to the operating centre.

Commissioners should ask non-participating providers to justify non-participation and require them to assess outcomes for all surgeons and centres against national benchmarks, report the findings and make them public.

Regulators should expect participation or an explanation for non-participation, consult centre and surgeon audit results during relevant inspections, and ensure quality assurance is performed by both NHS and independent providers.
limitations: Participation is incomplete. The authors state that national outcomes remain uncertain until all centres join and that unwarranted variation could exist among non-participating centres.

Completeness of VA data varies substantially between centres; only 64.4% of eligible eyes in the postoperative assessment period had both preoperative and postoperative measurements. This may conceal poor visual outcomes and limits the reliability and availability of Vision Loss results.
Vision Loss analyses exclude operations near the end of the audit year to allow postoperative follow-up; they consequently use a smaller sample than PCR analyses.
Operative complication reporting depends on surgeons' records and has no external validation, although the audit performs internal cross-checks.

The audit cannot currently link records collected at different centres or match patient records across systems when a centre changes its data-collection system. Missing first-eye records and system changes can affect results, particularly VA results.

Age and deprivation information depends on data available through participating centres' administrative or clinical systems; deprivation could not be calculated for all data sources or for centres using different national indices.

Results based on small numbers have substantial statistical uncertainty and potential bias. The authors also caution that the observed reduction in trainee-performed operations may not fully represent the national situation.
strengths: The audit covers 481,530 eligible operations at 177 centres and captures approximately 79.9% of NHS-funded phacoemulsification cataract operations in England and Wales for the 2022 NHS year.
Recording of the PCR outcome is approximately 100% complete for reported operations because operative complication status is a mandatory EMR field.
Case-complexity adjustment allows centres and surgeons undertaking more complex cases to benchmark outcomes against peers.
Integrated EMR audit tools permit local, real-time monitoring of adverse surgical events and can support prompt investigation and corrective action.
open_questions: Whether incomplete VA recording is concealing poor visual outcomes remains uncertain.
The quality and variation of cataract-surgery outcomes at centres that do not participate in the audit remain uncertain.
The authors note that the decline in trainee-performed operations may not fully reflect the national situation; both training case numbers and case complexity require monitoring.
future_directions: The audit aims to extend participation toward complete United Kingdom coverage, including centres in Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland as electronic data collection becomes available.
Future data extractions are planned later in the year so postoperative results can cover the complete reported NHS year.
The audit is considering additional, more patient-focused outcomes and is promoting collection of PROM; feasibility work on integrating CatPROM5 into EMR is under way.
A refitted PCR case-complexity adjustment model is planned to replace the existing model for audit year 8; the Vision Loss risk-factor model will be reviewed when resources permit.
The RCOphth NOD has applied for section 251 exemption to enable record linkage for patients presenting with complications or receiving care at multiple centres.

subgroup_analyses: In the 2022 NHS year, consultant surgeons performed 406,620 (84.4%) operations, career grade non-consultant surgeons 19,397 (4.0%), more experienced trainee surgeons 49,615 (10.3%), and less experienced trainee surgeons 5,898 (1.2%). The respective recorded PCR counts and rates were 2,456 (0.6%), 315 (1.6%), 878 (1.8%), and 137 (2.3%).

For 94,546 patients whose first and second treated eyes both had preoperative VA measured during the 2022 NHS year, excluding ISBCS, first treated eyes had a mean presenting VA 0.15 LogMAR units worse than second treated eyes (95% CI: 0.148 to 0.154 LogMAR); the respective means were 0.55 (6/21) and 0.40 LogMAR (6/15), p <0.001.
The median preoperative VA was 0.40 LogMAR units for eyes operated on by qualified surgeons and 0.50 LogMAR units for eyes operated on by trainee surgeons.

Among 238,248 patients in the social-deprivation analysis, preoperative VA of ≥1.00 LogMAR was recorded for 21.9% in the most deprived decile (decile 1) and 10.1% in the least deprived decile (decile 10). The report describes an association between greater deprivation and worse preoperative VA.

Among 1,523 ISCBS patients with preoperative VA for both eyes, the median difference between the better- and worse-seeing eyes was 0.00 LogMAR units; 557 (36.6%) had equal preoperative VA in both eyes.

Postoperative VA of 0.30 LogMAR (6/12 or better) was achieved by 95.8% of 151,964 eyes without an ocular co-pathology / risk indicator and 86.2% of 99,997 eyes with one, within the 251,961-eye paired-VA analysis.

Postoperative VA of 0.30 LogMAR (6/12 or better) was achieved by 92.2% of 247,925 eyes without an intraoperative complication and 76.0% of 4,036 eyes with one, within the 251,961-eye paired-VA analysis.
Postoperative VA of 0.30 LogMAR (6/12 or better) was achieved by 92.2% of 249,747 eyes without PCR and 71.1% of 2,214 eyes with PCR, within the 251,961-eye paired-VA analysis.
Among eyes with preoperative VA of ≤0.00 LogMAR, 74.7% had postoperative VA of ≤0.00 LogMAR; among eyes with preoperative VA of ≤0.30 LogMAR, 97.8% had postoperative VA of ≤0.30 LogMAR.

Postoperative VA data were available for 72.4% of first treated eyes and 64.0% of second treated eyes. In 148 (86.0%) centres, completeness was higher for first treated eyes; the difference exceeded 10% points in 50 (29.1%) centres and 25% points in 18 (10.5%) centres.

Of 15,643 (6.2%) eyes with paired VA measurements and preoperative VA worse than 1.30 LogMAR, 14,490 (92.6%) improved beyond the severely sight impaired certification VA threshold and 1,153 (7.4%) remained worse than 1.30 LogMAR. Of 236,318 (93.8%) eyes with preoperative VA of 1.30 LogMAR or better, 376 (0.2%) worsened to the certification VA threshold; these estimates use VA rather than visual-field measurements.

Excluding ISBCS eyes, severe VA loss occurred in 335 (0.22%) of 155,503 first treated eyes and 196 (0.21%) of 93,767 second treated eyes. Among 505 ISBCS patients (1,010 eyes), it occurred in 1 (<0.1%) eye.

During the postoperative complication assessment period, 82,473 patients underwent surgery in both eyes, excluding ISBCS. Postoperative CMO affected 712 (0.86%) first treated eyes, 803 (0.97%) second treated eyes, and both eyes of 133 (0.16%) patients. Postoperative uveitis affected 1,623 (1.97%) first treated eyes, 1,711 (2.07%) second treated eyes, and both eyes of 280 (0.34%) patients. Postoperative endophthalmitis affected three first treated eyes and 16 (0.02%) second treated eyes; no patient developed it in both eyes.

For 1,389 ISBCS patients (2,778 eyes) in the postoperative assessment period, seven eyes developed postoperative uveitis, seven developed postoperative CMO, and no eyes developed postoperative endophthalmitis. Postoperative CMO occurred in both eyes of three patients, and postoperative uveitis in both eyes of two patients.

Among 1,643 ISBCS patients in the 2022 NHS year, 164 (10.0%) underwent general anaesthesia. The corresponding proportions were 38.2% and 44.7% in the 2018 and 2019 NHS years, 9.0% in the 2020 NHS year, and 10.1% in the 2021 NHS year.
secondary_results: The audit received data for 496,031 NHS-funded phacoemulsification cataract operations in England and Wales, approximately 79.9% of such operations during the 2022 NHS year. Overall, 502,183 operations were submitted by 180 centres; 499,662 (99.5%) used phacoemulsification. After excluding 20,595 (4.1%) operations and a further 58 operations from three centres with <50 eligible operations, 481,530 operations from 177 centres remained.
Among 157 centres for which case ascertainment could be estimated, the overall estimate was 96.0%; 143 (91.1%) centres exceeded 90%, and centre estimates ranged from 3.5% to 100%.

Eligible operations involved 367,515 patients and comprised 239,281 (49.7%) left eyes and 242,249 (50.3%) right eyes. English centres performed 477,340 (99.1%) operations, Welsh centres 3,679 (0.8%), and Guernsey 511 (0.1%).

Among 481,019 operations in England or Wales, 165,983 (34.5%) took place in traditional NHS centres, 311,927 (64.9%) were NHS-funded surgery at ISTC sites, and 3,109 (0.7%) were private fee-paying operations.

A total of 2,312 surgeons performed eligible operations. The median number per surgeon was 65 (IQR; 24 – 144: range; 1 – 7,279); 1,343 (58.1%) surgeons had ≥50 eligible operations and 102 had >1,000 operations.

First treated-eye surgery accounted for 280,357 (58.6%) operations, with median patient age 76.0 years (IQR; 69.4 – 81.5). Second treated-eye surgery accounted for 197,887 (41.4%) operations, with median patient age 76.7 years (IQR; 70.7 – 82.2). ISBCS was performed in 1,643 patients by 295 surgeons at 64 centres; median patient age was 73.7 years (IQR; 66.0 – 79.6).
Preoperative VA was 0.30 LogMAR units (6/12) or better for 168,522 (40.5%) eyes, 0.60 LogMAR units (6/24) or better for 314,714 (75.6%), and 1.0 LogMAR units (6/60) or better for 378,649 (91.0%).
Postoperative VA was 0.60 LogMAR units (6/24) or better for 262,742 (97.3%) eyes and 1.0 LogMAR units (6/60) or better for 267,534 (99.0%) eyes among those eligible for postoperative VA assessment.
Among eyes eligible for change-in-VA analysis, 19,751 (7.8%) had a change of ±0.10 LogMAR (±1 Snellen line). For all bar two centres, median postoperative VA was better than median preoperative VA.

An ocular co-pathology or known risk factor was recorded as present for 170,902 (35.5%) eyes and absent or not recorded for 310,628 (64.5%); the latter grouping assumes unrecorded status means none. Status was recorded for 94.0% of operated eyes and unrecorded for 6.0%.

The most frequently recorded ocular co-pathologies or risk factors were age-related macular degeneration in 7.4% of operations, Corneal pathology in 7.1%, unspecified ‘other’ in 5.6%, and glaucoma in 5.6% according to the detailed-results prose. The appendix table instead lists Glaucoma at 5.3% for the 2022 NHS year.

Phacoemulsification ± IOL was the sole operative procedure in 459,151 (95.4%) operations, was combined with one other procedure in 20,239 (4.2%), and with ≥2 other procedures in 2,140 (0.4%). The most frequent additions were insertion of pupil ring expander in 1.4%, intraoperative phenylephrine in 0.9%, and anterior vitrectomy in 0.5% of operations.

The appendix reports 6,531 instances of insertion of pupil ring expander, 4,231 of intraoperative phenylephrine, 2,233 of automated anterior vitrectomy, 2,020 of insertion of Iris hooks, and 1,837 of capsular tension ring alongside phacoemulsification ± IOL.

Of 391,598 operations available for postoperative-complication assessment, 133,364 (34.1%) had ‘none’ recorded as the postoperative complication, while 233,455 (59.6%) had no postoperative-complication record.
The proportion of operations contributed by consultant surgeons rose from 70.5% in the 2018 NHS year to 84.4% in the 2022 NHS year.

The audit estimates that the reduction in recorded PCR since 2010 corresponds to approximately 7,000 fewer complications annually across the NHS and around £3.5 million in annual savings from avoided additional treatments.

main_conclusion: The authors judge cataract surgery across the 177 participating centres to be of generally good quality, with recorded PCR and assessable Vision Loss lower than in 2010. They caution that incomplete and variable VA recording prevents confidence that poor visual outcomes are not being missed, while declining trainee participation raises concern for future service sustainability.
narrative_summary: This prospective national audit assessed adult cataract operations involving phacoemulsification during the 2022 NHS year, using routinely collected records from participating centres. Of 502,183 submitted operations, 481,530 from 177 centres were eligible. Surgical quality was evaluated principally through PCR and Vision Loss, with centre results adjusted for case complexity. The unadjusted PCR rate was 0.79%; assessable Vision Loss was 0.48%. Compared with 2010, the report describes reductions of around 58% in recorded PCR and 31% in assessable Vision Loss. No surgeons or centres exceeded the national threshold by more than 3 standard deviations for either outcome. Among eyes eligible for postoperative VA assessment, 91.8% achieved VA of 0.30 LogMAR or better. However, only 64.4% of eyes in the qualifying postoperative period had both preoperative and postoperative VA recorded. The authors therefore caution that variation in VA completeness could conceal poor visual outcomes; centres without sufficient paired measurements were not given Vision Loss rates. Eyes with ocular co-pathology, an intraoperative complication or PCR had worse postoperative VA than their respective comparison groups. Greater social deprivation was associated with worse preoperative VA. Trainees performed 11.5% of eligible operations in 2022, down from 21.9% in 2018, prompting concern about training capacity. The report calls for fuller outcome and risk-factor recording, continued quality monitoring and attention to surgical training.

document_sections.heading: National Ophthalmology Database Audit
document_sections.content: The seventh annual National Cataract Audit report covers the 2022 NHS year, from 01 April 2022 to 31 March 2023.

document_sections.heading: Foreword
document_sections.content: Audit coverage grew from 68,107 cataract operations at 42 centres in 2010 to 481,530 operations at 177 centres, including independent treatment centres, between April 2022 and March 2023. The foreword identifies posterior capsule rupture (PCR) and surgery-related visual loss as patient-centred quality measures. PCR is described as an internationally recognised surgical quality marker and a major risk factor for retinal detachment and endophthalmitis; its rate has fallen by 58% since 2010 to 0.79%. Visual-loss risk has fallen by 31% since 2010 to 0.48%. The improvements are attributed at least partly to clinicians and centres reviewing and changing practice, alongside developments in phacoemulsification equipment. Both preoperative and postoperative visual acuity (VA) were documented for only 64.4% of operations; the foreword links this concern partly to communication between primary and secondary care. It also warns that the significant fall in trainee-performed operations relative to pre-COVID affects training and risks future service safety and quality. Patients and providers are encouraged to examine surgeon and centre results on the NOD website. Clinicians should discuss the audit’s main outcomes during consent and use patient-specific PCR risk calculations as recommended by NICE cataract surgery guideline (NG77). The audit aims ultimately to cover the whole United Kingdom and to use its findings to improve care.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Context
document_sections.content: Cataract surgery was the most frequent NHS surgical procedure. During the 2022 NHS year, approximately 608,000 publicly funded operations took place in England and 16,000 in Wales; estimated annual NHS expenditure was around £600 million. This prospective report includes operations from 01 April 2022 to 31 March 2023. The audit assesses whether PCR and Vision Loss rates meet quality standards. Compared with the 2010 proof of concept, recorded PCR has fallen by around 58% and assessable Vision Loss by 31%, corresponding to approximately 7,000 fewer complications annually across the NHS and estimated avoided-treatment savings of around £3.5 million per year. It presents case-complexity-adjusted PCR and monocular Vision Loss rates for named centres, including all surgeons; centre findings also go to the Care Quality Commission (CQC). Vision Loss rates are withheld when <60% of outcome data are available because they are considered unreliable. Institutions are included when the specified clinical and information-governance authorities have approved use of their data.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Aims
document_sections.content: The audit seeks to assure the quality of cataract surgery for patients whose cataract-related visual impairment leads them to undergo an operation, flagging performance below reasonable patient expectations. It also aims to support quality improvement through feedback on complications. Its two primary patient-safety measures are risk-adjusted PCR and Vision Loss. Operative-complication recording is mandatory in ophthalmology EMR systems, so PCR data should be highly complete; preoperative risk information and follow-up VA may be less complete because pathways and EMR use differ. Reporting adjusted PCR is intended to encourage preoperative risk profiling and prevention of avoidable complications. Reporting Vision Loss is intended to reveal potentially preventable visual harm and unwarranted variation. Secondary measures include case complexity, valid VA recording, access to surgery measured through preoperative VA, and deprivation.

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Audit measures
document_sections.content: The primary operative outcome, PCR, comprises posterior capsule rupture with or without vitreous prolapse or zonule rupture accompanied by vitreous prolapse. Surgery-related Vision Loss means at least a doubling of the visual angle, equivalent to losing three or more lines or 15 or more letters on a LogMAR chart. Centre outcomes are risk-adjusted and accompanied by information on operative volume, completeness, complexity, access and deprivation. EMR systems permit local, real-time surveillance, potentially allowing prompt responses to adverse signals. Adjusted results also allow centres and surgeons to compare performance with peers and review practice when outcomes are worse.

document_sections.heading: 1.3.1 Posterior capsular rupture
document_sections.content: NICE cataract surgery guideline (NG77) highlights PCR as a surgical risk, and the International Consortium for Health Outcome Measurement (ICHOM) uses it as an adverse surgical outcome. It occurs on average in approximately one operation in 100, although preoperative patient and eye factors can change risk by as much as fifty-fold. PCR significantly increases the risk of ocular harm and can impede visual recovery. When it occurs, the report cites an approximate 20-fold risk of retinal detachment during the year after surgery, 17-fold risk of acute intra-operative supra-choroidal haemorrhage, 16-fold risk of losing ≥0.6 LogMAR from before to after surgery, 7-fold risk of postoperative endophthalmitis, and 6-fold risk of losing ≥0.3 LogMAR.

document_sections.heading: 1.3.2 Vision Loss
document_sections.content: Surgery-related Vision Loss is contrary to the intended surgical benefit and, together with PCR, measures safety-related aspects of quality. NICE cataract surgery guideline (NG77) identifies Vision Loss as a surgical risk. Assessment requires VA before and after surgery, making missing VA information consequential. The reference rates used for risk adjustment, established in the second prospective audit year from unadjusted consultant-surgeon outcomes, are 1.10% for PCR and 0.90% for VA Loss. This is the last annual report to use those references: a refitted PCR model and updated reference values are planned for the 2023-24 audit year.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Participation
document_sections.content: The report covers 177 centres: 172 in England, four in Wales and one in Guernsey. Of these, 135 used EMR and 42 used in-house or bespoke collection. Among 114 eligible NHS organisations in England and Wales, 73 (64.0%) were represented. Data also came from nine independent-sector providers of NHS-funded services operating 102 sites, one Guernsey centre and one private provider. One NHS trust and one independent-sector provider comprising 22 sites submitted both NHS-funded and private fee-paying operations. NHS Digital received records of 608,120 English and 16,338 Welsh phacoemulsification cataract operations for the 2022 NHS year. The audit received 496,031 NHS-funded operations of this type from England and Wales, approximately 79.9% of the corresponding operations. Around 4% were excluded, including operations undertaken for purposes other than visual improvement or combined with substantial intraocular surgery; 481,530 eligible operations remained.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Data Quality
document_sections.content: PCR ascertainment for submitted operations was around 100%, reflecting its mandatory EMR field. Eligible preoperative distance VA was recorded for 85.5% of eyes, postoperative VA for 69.0%, and both measurements for 64.4%. Completeness differed significantly between centres, in association with differences in EMR use, care pathways and recovery after COVID 19 service disruption in the 2020 NHS year.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Posterior Capsular Rupture
document_sections.content: Across all surgeons, PCR was recorded in 0.79% of operations, approximately 58% less than in 2010.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 Vision Loss
document_sections.content: Postoperative VA of 0.30 LogMAR (=6/12, required to drive) or better occurred in 91.8% of eyes overall, 95.8% without ocular co-pathology and 86.2% with a recorded co-pathology. Median preoperative VA was 0.40 LogMAR units (6/15 Snellen equivalent), median postoperative VA was 0.10 LogMAR units (6/7.5 Snellen), and median improvement was 0.30 LogMAR. Assessable Vision Loss was 0.48%, approximately 31% below its 2010 level. Its analysis used fewer operations than the PCR analysis because some preoperative or postoperative VA measurements were absent and operations in the final two months of the audit year were excluded to allow postoperative follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Table 1: Audit estimates for different NHS years where each year represents the time period of 01 April to 31 March
document_sections.content: The table tracks participating centres, eligible operations, case ascertainment, unadjusted PCR and VA Loss, and completeness of VA data across NHS years. Centres did not necessarily contribute in consecutive extractions, some merged, and initial submissions could cover less than a full year. The first audit year ran from 01 September 2015 to 31 August 2016; years 2, 3 and 4 followed corresponding periods in 2016/17, 2017/18 and 2018/19. From year 5, the audit followed 01 April to 31 March. Newly participating centres could submit historical records from 01 April 2010. Case ascertainment compares audit submissions with centrally reported operations, with a pro rata denominator for centres that began recording partway through the period. Centres submitting more cases than the central comparator were treated as completely ascertained because their actual ascertainment could not be estimated. Ascertainment estimates were unavailable for the 2010 to 2015 NHS years because the necessary central data were not received.

document_sections.heading: 3. Summary
document_sections.content: The audit captures over 79% of NHS-funded cataract operations in England and Wales and reports 177 centres, including 71 English NHS trusts, two Welsh Local Health Boards, nine independent-sector providers operating 102 sites, a Guernsey centre and a private provider. Surgeon and centre findings are available publicly. PCR and Vision Loss are established, risk-adjusted measures of surgical quality; Vision Loss captures adverse visual outcomes whether or not PCR occurred. In the 2022 NHS year, no surgeon or centre was more than 3 standard deviations above the national threshold for either outcome. Since 2010, PCR has fallen by around 58% and Vision Loss by 31%; the PCR reduction represents approximately 7,000 fewer NHS complications and approximately £3.5 million in avoided annual costs. Trainees performed 21.9% of eligible operations in the 2018 NHS year versus 11.5% in the 2022 NHS year, partly because high-volume consultant-delivered services without surgical training became more prominent in the database. Training-case availability and complexity in training institutions require monitoring to protect future services. Case ascertainment is high at most centres, with notable exceptions. PCR recording is described as 100% complete, whereas postoperative VA information is less complete; centres and surgeons recording VA in fewer than 60% of cases cannot be assessed for that outcome. Better postoperative recording is needed. Risk adjustment acknowledges case complexity, but incomplete risk-factor entries can prevent surgeons and centres receiving appropriate recognition for complex work. Across five NHS years, 196 centres submitted at least 50 eligible operations in a year; 146 used EMR and 50 used in-house databases. EMR tools can support real-time recognition of adverse trends and timely corrective action.

document_sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors judge publicly funded cataract surgery at the 177 participating centres to be of generally good quality. Since feedback to surgeons and centres began in 2010, recorded PCR has fallen by around 58% and assessable Vision Loss by 31%, with reduced morbidity for over 7,000 patients annually and estimated NHS savings of around £3.5 million each year from avoided complications. The audit seeks participation from every publicly funded provider; this report includes nine independent-sector providers with 102 sites. Until coverage is complete, national outcomes remain uncertain and unwarranted variation at nonparticipating centres remains possible. Broader, more patient-focused outcomes are under consideration. The more even distribution of operations across months of the 2022 NHS year suggests recovery after COVID-19 disruption: monthly proportions in 2021 and 2022 resembled 2018 and 2019 more than the heavily disrupted 2020 NHS year. Trainee-performed operations reported to NOD almost halved between 2018 and 2022; although this might not represent the national position fully, it raises concern about investment in training and service sustainability. Variation in completeness of VA recording prevents confidence that poor visual outcomes are not being missed.

document_sections.heading: 1. Recommendations for Patients
document_sections.content: Patients, carers and others interested in cataract surgery are encouraged to consult quality information about local services on the National Ophthalmology Database Audit website. Patients whose local provider does not participate could ask their hospital through PALS why it does not participate and request outcome information for comparison with national benchmarks.

document_sections.heading: 2. Recommendations for Providers of cataract surgery
document_sections.content: All NHS cataract providers should contribute data to the audit to demonstrate their commitment to quality and professional practice. Providers should review their centre results, agree quality-improvement and data-collection actions, and submit complete information, including relevant risk factors, so case complexity can be considered under the UK Minimum Cataract Dataset for National Audit. They should use electronic collection and EMR audit tools for continuous real-time surveillance and early correction of potential problems. They should review pathways to maximise preoperative and postoperative VA recording for every operation and aim to collect postoperative refractive outcomes routinely. They should consider preoperative and postoperative Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs), as advised by the 2019 NICE Quality standard for serious eye disorders (QS180), to quantify and validate patient benefit.

document_sections.heading: 3. Recommendations for Commissioners
document_sections.content: The document additionally asks EMR-enabled providers to review mandatory-field settings, mandate recording the surgeon GMC number as part of the legal clinical record, and check trainee details annually to ensure grades are accurate. Surgeons at nonparticipating centres should approach senior management about the quality-assurance, improvement, accountability, public-perception and commissioning benefits of joining. Commissioners should include complete RCOphth NOD submissions, including preoperative and postoperative VA, in quality-focused contracts for both NHS and independent providers of NHS-funded surgery, consistent with NHS England’s 2022 Supplementary Cataract Contracting guidance. Where postoperative care is outsourced, services should require VA and refraction data to return to the operating centre through available tools. Nonparticipating providers should be asked to justify nonparticipation and required to conduct surgeon- and centre-level quality assurance against national benchmarks, report it to commissioners and publish the results, as indicated in NICE cataract surgery guideline (NG77).

document_sections.heading: 4. Recommendations for the Regulators
document_sections.content: Regulators should expect NHS cataract providers either to join the NOD Cataract Audit or explain nonparticipation; participation is obligatory in England because the audit appears on the NHS England Quality Accounts List. When inspecting organisations that commission or provide cataract surgery, regulators should examine audit findings for centres and surgeons. They should ensure quality assurance is undertaken by every NHS cataract-surgery provider, including independent and nonparticipating providers.

document_sections.heading: 6. Future of the audit
document_sections.content: Continuation of the national audit is planned while participating-centre funding and data, supplemented by industry donations, remain available. An extraction planned for June/July 2024 will underpin the eighth prospective annual report. Later future extractions are intended to allow postoperative findings for a complete NHS year. Northern Irish centres are expected to begin participating after EMR implementation; EMR procurement in Wales and Scotland is expected to enable wider participation there. As cataract surgery increasingly occurs earlier in disease with better VA, RCOphth NOD aims to promote patient-reported outcomes; feasibility work on integrating CatPROM5 into EMR is underway. In 2023, RCOphth NOD issued its first national wet age-related macular degeneration audit report, and many centres participate in both audits. The audit has applied for section 251 exemption to enable NHS-number submission and linkage of records across centres or after complications. A refitted PCR case-complexity model is planned to replace the current model in audit year 8; the Vision Loss risk-factor model will be reviewed when resources permit.

document_sections.heading: Appendix A: Audit Framework
document_sections.content: The report concerns adult cataract operations involving phacoemulsification. Data came from Medisoft EMR at 127 centres, Open Eyes EMR at six, both Medisoft and OpenEyes EMR at one, Epic at one, and in-house or bespoke systems at 42. PCR analyses cover 01 April 2022 to 31 March 2023. Risk-adjusted Vision Loss, postoperative complications and postoperative VA cover 01 April 2022 to 31 January 2023 to allow recovery and postoperative data collection. Exclusions include operations without phacoemulsification; operations combined with another substantial intraocular procedure, such as trabeculectomy, minimally invasive glaucoma surgery or pars plana vitrectomy with other vitreoretinal procedures; previously traumatised eyes; polar cataracts; significant congenital or developmental ocular abnormalities; and patients aged <18 years.

document_sections.heading: B.1 Context of the data collection
document_sections.content: Audit information arises from routine cataract-service records. EMR integration means most centres can collect it without extra staff work, whereas some non-EMR centres require additional effort. Complication reporting depends on accurate surgeon entries and lacks external validation, although postoperative findings and subsequent procedures permit internal checks. EMR operation notes require a specific ‘Yes / No’ response about complications and constitute the medicolegal operative record. Other fields vary in completeness: theatre-only electronic use can omit outpatient information, and postoperative VA and refraction often depend on an optometrist returning measurements to the hospital. The audit encourages links with community optometrists and provides a web-based return tool. Newly implemented EMR systems may have a lag before complete service-wide use, affecting initial submissions.

document_sections.heading: B.2 Case ascertainment
document_sections.content: The estimated share of cataract operations submitted to the audit uses centrally reported counts from NHS Digital or Digital Health and Care Wales (DHCW), with pro rata adjustment for recently joined centres. Because the audit subsequently excludes some operations, this comparison uses submitted phacoemulsification operations before applying audit exclusions.

document_sections.heading: B.3 Data quality and completeness
document_sections.content: Mandatory EMR fields and automatic range checks can improve completeness and accuracy. Other EMR information permits cross-checks. Preoperative and postoperative VA completeness varies substantially and needs improvement at many centres. A web-based tool supports community optometrists in returning postoperative results; the report notes that commissioned community follow-up can link payment to receipt of data by the surgical centre.

document_sections.heading: B.4 Small numbers policy
document_sections.content: Centres contributing <50 eligible operations are excluded from the report. Centre-level vision estimates also exclude centres with <50 eligible operations with VA measurements; postoperative centre results are not generated where the qualifying postoperative period contains <50 eligible operations.

document_sections.heading: B.5 Outliers policy
document_sections.content: For this one-year report, a centre or surgeon is classified as an outlier if its risk-adjusted adverse-event rate exceeds the national threshold by approximately three Standard Deviations (3SD), consistent with the stated NHS England national-audit policy.

document_sections.heading: B.6 Limitations of the data
document_sections.content: Records include first eyes, second eyes and some immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery (ISBCS), but a first-eye record may be absent if surgery preceded electronic collection or occurred elsewhere. The audit cannot currently link records collected at different centres. When a centre changes systems during an audit year, records from the two systems cannot be matched; preoperative and postoperative VA may therefore be separated, affecting results. Three centres in this report changed EMR during the year. Age and deprivation information depend on administrative-system entries and their links to EMR. Deprivation information came from most Medisoft EMR operations and one in-house database, but not other data sources; the audit is working to improve its availability.

document_sections.heading: C.1 Dataset
document_sections.content: The audit specifies a minimum cataract dataset that includes variables needed to adjust outcomes for case complexity.

document_sections.heading: C.2 Surgeon grade
document_sections.content: Surgeons are grouped as consultant surgeons; career grade non-consultant surgeons, comprising associate specialists, staff grade and trust doctors; experienced trainees, including fellows, registrars, speciality registrars years 3 – 7 and specialty trainees years 3 – 7; and less experienced trainees, including SHO, specialty registrars years 1 – 2, specialty trainees years 1 – 2 and foundation doctors years 1 – 2.

document_sections.heading: C.3 Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR)
document_sections.content: For this audit, PCR includes a tear of the posterior capsule regardless of vitreous prolapse, or zonular rupture with vitreous prolapse. Zonular dehiscence without vitreous prolapse is excluded. The measure is intended to identify a clinically important breach of the lens–zonule barrier.

document_sections.heading: C.4 Visual Acuity (VA)
document_sections.content: VA definitions specify preoperative and postoperative measurement windows and preferences among corrected, uncorrected and pinhole measurements to make use of available information. Centre-specific VA completeness across different windows is presented in Appendix U.

document_sections.heading: C.5 Mixed effects modelling of PCR and Vision Loss
document_sections.content: Mixed effects logistic regression models for PCR and Vision Loss were developed using operations from the four-year period covering the 2011-12 to 2014-15 NHS years. Their equations were applied to this report’s outcomes. Case-mix-adjusted plots use 95% and 99.8% error lines based on earlier overall consultant rates of 1.1% for PCR and 0.9% for Vision Loss. A centre or surgeon needs at least 50 eligible operations for a result; Vision Loss reporting additionally requires both VA measurements for at least 60% of operations. Centre-level adjusted PCR plots include trainees, with adjustment for their results.

document_sections.heading: C.6 Case complexity index
document_sections.content: Each centre receives separate PCR and Vision Loss case-complexity indices. Each index represents the model-predicted overall probability of the corresponding adverse outcome given the complexity recorded for that centre’s cases.

document_sections.heading: D.1 Case ascertainment
document_sections.content: A total of 502,183 operations were submitted by 180 centres; 499,662 (99.5%) used phacoemulsification. Three centres were excluded because each supplied <50 eligible operations. Two centres were not required to report to NHS Digital or DHCW, and NHS Digital comparator data were unavailable for 18 centres. Among 157 centres for which ascertainment could be estimated, overall ascertainment was 96.0%; 143 (91.1%) centres exceeded 90%, and individual estimates ranged from 3.5% to 100%. Of the 502,183 submitted operations, 20,595 (4.1%) were excluded from analysis, plus 58 operations from three centres below the <50 threshold. The resulting 481,530 eligible operations came from 177 centres and involved 367,515 patients: 239,281 (49.7%) left eyes and 242,249 (50.3%) right eyes. English centres performed 477,340 (99.1%) operations, Welsh centres 3,679 (0.8%), and Guernsey 511 (0.1%). Among 481,019 operations in England or Wales, 165,983 (34.5%) occurred at traditional NHS centres, 311,927 (64.9%) were NHS-funded at ISTC sites, and 3,109 (0.7%) were privately funded.

document_sections.heading: D.2 Surgeons
document_sections.content: The 481,530 eligible operations involved 2,312 surgeons. The report records 1,244 consultants performing 406,620 (84.4%) operations; 217 career grade non-consultants performing 19,397 (4.0%); 807 more experienced trainees performing 49,615 (10.3%); and 151 less experienced trainees performing 5,898 (1.2%). The number of operations per surgeon had a median of 65 operations (IQR; 24 – 144: range; 1 – 7,279). Comparative medians were 65, 67, 34 and 57 for the 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021 NHS years. In 2022, 102 surgeons had >1,000 operations: one worked solely in NHS trusts, 61 solely at ISTC sites, and 40 in both settings. Overall, 1,343 (58.1%) surgeons had ≥50 eligible operations, compared with 57.9%, 59.4%, 37.9% and 53.6% in the 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021 NHS years. Of 969 (41.9%) surgeons with <50 operations, 492 (50.8%) were consultants or independent non-consultants, 465 (48.0%) were trainees, and 12 (1.2%) had records in both categories. Surgeon gender was recorded as male for 1,479 (64.0%), female for 821 (35.5%) and unknown for 12 (0.5%). Data spanned two centres for 414 (17.9%) surgeons, three for 67 (2.9%), and four or more for 137 (5.9%); 41 had >10 centres, eight had ≥20 and two had ≥30. Among those with >10 centres, 18 had one NHS trust plus ISTC sites and 23 had only ISTC sites. Among the eight with ≥20 centres, six had one NHS trust plus ISTC sites and two had only ISTC sites. Of the two with ≥30 centres, one had 32 ISTC sites and no NHS trust; the other had 34 ISTC sites and one NHS trust. Consultant-performed operations rose from 70.5% in 2018 to 84.4% in 2022, partly reflecting greater ISTC representation. Trainee-performed operations fell by around 47%, from 21.9% to 11.5%. The report relates unusual surgeon-volume patterns in 2020 to COVID-19 disruption and regards 2022 as showing some recovery. Surgeons with >1,000 operations were approximately eight times as numerous in 2022 as in 2018 and four-times as numerous as in 2020, partly because high-volume ISTC surgeons were increasingly represented.

document_sections.heading: D.3 Patient characteristics – age and gender
document_sections.content: Among 367,515 patients, 152,957 (41.6%) were men and 210,555 (57.3%) were women; gender was unrecorded for 4,002 (1.1%), and one patient had gender recorded as indeterminate / anticipated sex change. Ethnicity was unrecorded for 174,796 (47.6%). Characteristics of patients undergoing first- and second-eye surgery were described as very similar.

document_sections.heading: D.4 First eye, second eye and ISBCS eyes
document_sections.content: An operation was classified as involving a first or second treated eye unless the patient underwent ISBCS. Records for both operations may not be available when an eye was treated elsewhere, before electronic collection, or in a different system at the same centre. The report therefore gives no interval between first- and second-eye surgery. It describes patients’ characteristics separately for first eyes, second eyes and ISBCS eyes. Across NHS years, characteristics of first- and second-eye patients were broadly similar, while recorded diabetes and use of general anaesthesia showed signs of decreasing. ISBCS comparisons across years were affected partly by small earlier samples. General anaesthesia in ISBCS was reported for 38.2% and 44.7% in the 2018 and 2019 NHS years, fell to 9.0% in 2020, and remained at around 10% thereafter; the report suggests a practice change during COVID 19 disruption persisted.

document_sections.heading: First treated eye cataract surgery;
document_sections.content: First-eye surgery accounted for 280,357 (58.6%) operations. Median age was 76.0 years (IQR; 69.4 – 81.5). At first surgery, 29,023 (10.4%) patients had recorded diabetes mellitus, 3,453 (1.2%) could not lie flat, and 6,601 (2.4%) could not cooperate during surgery. General anaesthesia was used for 6,119 (2.2%) patients, including 5,528 who also received local and/or topical anaesthesia.

document_sections.heading: Second treated eye cataract surgery;
document_sections.content: Second-eye surgery comprised 197,887 (41.4%) operations. Median age was 76.7 years (IQR; 70.7 – 82.2). Recorded diabetes mellitus affected 21,974 (11.1%) patients; 2,034 (1.0%) could not lie flat and 5,218 (2.6%) could not cooperate. General anaesthesia was used for 4,462 (2.3%) patients, including 4,137 who also received local and/or topical anaesthesia.

document_sections.heading: ISBCS eyes;
document_sections.content: ISBCS involved 1,643 patients, 295 surgeons and 64 centres. The same surgeon operated on both eyes in 1,458 (88.7%) patients. A trainee performed 324 (19.7%) of the operations, and trainees operated on both eyes in 90 (5.5%) patients. Median patient age was 73.7 years (IQR; 66.0 – 79.6); reported mean ages were 72.6 for males and 71.7 for females. There were 710 (43.2%) male and 931 (56.7%) female patients, while gender was unrecorded for 2 (0.1%). Diabetes mellitus was recorded for 204 (12.4%); 50 (3.0%) could not lie flat and 42 (2.6%) could not cooperate. General anaesthesia was used in 164 (10.0%) patients, including 141 who also received local or topical anaesthesia.

document_sections.heading: D.5 Index of multiple deprivation
document_sections.content: The English deprivation index was available for 265,984 (97.8%) patients from 125 English centres: 124 contributed Medisoft EMR data and one an in-house database. All but two centres operated on patients in the most deprived national decile (decile 1), and all but two treated patients in the least deprived decile (decile 10). Median deprivation decile differed significantly between centres. The index could not be calculated for other contributing collection systems or for Welsh and Channel Island centres, which use different indices.

document_sections.heading: D.6 Preoperative Visual Acuity (VA)
document_sections.content: Preoperative VA was recorded for 416,311 (86.5%) of 481,530 eligible operations and absent for 65,219 (13.5%); among all operations, 2,937 (0.6%) had PHVA but neither CDVA nor UDVA. Recording differed markedly between centres: 13 (7.3%) had preoperative VA for <50% of eyes, including two with none; 133 (75.1%) exceeded 80%, and 84 (47.5%) exceeded 95%. Comparable overall completeness was 90.0%, 85.7%, 70.8% and 86.2% for the 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021 NHS years. Among 416,311 measured eyes from 175 centres, the selected measure was CDVA in 294,439 (70.7%), UDVA in 114,601 (27.5%), and identical CDVA and UDVA in 7,271 (1.8%). Median preoperative VA was 0.40 LogMAR units (6/15 Snellen equivalent), with a range of -0.30 to NPL (6/3 to NPL Snellen equivalent). Vision was CF in 11,154 (2.7%) eyes, HM in 8,919 (2.1%), PL in 2,252 (0.5%) and NPL in 161 (<0.1%). Median VA was 0.40 LogMAR units in eyes operated on by qualified surgeons and 0.50 LogMAR units for trainee-operated eyes. Preoperative VA of 0.30 LogMAR units (6/12) or better occurred in 168,522 (40.5%) eyes; 0.60 LogMAR units (6/24) or better in 314,714 (75.6%); and 1.0 LogMAR units (6/60) or better in 378,649 (91.0%). At 52 (29.7%) centres, median preoperative VA was 0.50 LogMAR (6/19 Snellen equivalent). Centre medians ranged from 0.00 to 0.80 LogMAR (6/6 to 6/38 Snellen equivalent), and 169 (96.6%) fell between 0.30 and 0.60 LogMAR. Using preoperative VA as a proxy for cataract severity, the report finds greater deprivation associated with worse VA: ≥1.00 LogMAR occurred in 21.9% of patients in decile 1 versus 10.1% in decile 10. Among 94,546 patients who underwent non-ISBCS surgery in both eyes during the 2022 NHS year and had both preoperative measurements, first-eye mean presenting VA was 0.15 LogMAR units worse (95% CI: 0.148 to 0.154 LogMAR) than second-eye VA; respective means were 0.55 (6/21) and 0.40 LogMAR (6/15), p <0.001. The authors infer that first eyes are generally treated when cataract is more advanced. Among 1,523 ISCBS patients with measurements for both eyes, the median better–worse-eye difference was 0.00 LogMAR units, and 557 (36.6%) had equal preoperative VA.

document_sections.content: The table presents numbers of patients and percentages across preoperative LogMAR VA categories for deprivation deciles and the overall group.

document_sections.heading: D.7 Ocular co-pathologies and risk factors
document_sections.content: Ocular co-pathology or known-risk-factor status was entered for 94.0% of operated eyes and unrecorded for 6.0%. Treating unrecorded status as absence, 170,902 (35.5%) eyes had a co-pathology or risk factor and 310,628 (64.5%) did not have one recorded. The proportion with any co-pathology ranged by centre from 0.0% to 79.1%; at 52 (29.4%) centres it exceeded 50%, while two centres submitted all operations without a recorded co-pathology. The most commonly recorded conditions were age-related macular degeneration, Corneal pathology, unspecified ‘other’, and glaucoma, at 7.4%, 7.1%, 5.6% and 5.6% of operations, respectively. Consultants performed >60% of operations for each individual co-pathology. Centre-level variation persisted across NHS years; individual condition frequencies were stable for some conditions and variable for others.

document_sections.heading: D.8 Operation characteristics
document_sections.content: Phacoemulsification ± IOL was the sole procedure in 459,151 (95.4%) operations, accompanied by one other procedure in 20,239 (4.2%), and by ≥2 other procedures in 2,140 (0.4%). The most frequent accompanying procedures were insertion of pupil ring expander, intraoperative phenylephrine and anterior vitrectomy, performed in 1.4%, 0.9% and 0.5% of operations, respectively.

document_sections.heading: D.9 Operative complications
document_sections.content: At least one intraoperative complication was recorded in 7,642 (1.6%) operations. PCR was the most commonly recorded, affecting 3,786 (0.8%). Rates of any intraoperative complication were higher in less experienced surgeon grades. For most individual complications, rates were similar by grade, although some were more frequent in less experienced grades.

document_sections.heading: D.10 Case complexity adjusted PCR results
document_sections.content: The report presents unadjusted and case-complexity-adjusted PCR outcomes for 177 participating centres. None met the outlier definition in the 2022 NHS year. Centre-specific results and indices of predicted PCR probability are presented in Appendix N, with prior-year adjusted outcomes in Appendix T. Adjusted PCR findings are intended for public display for participating centres and fully qualified consultants or career grade non-consultants with at least 50 eligible operations. For this analysis, PCR includes posterior capsule rupture with or without vitreous prolapse and zonular rupture with vitreous prolapse; retained lens material in the vitreous implies PCR.
